asDecan.p: Every sign gets split into three decans of ten degrees, and each one has a planet running it and a small card of its own. Your Sun is in the first ten degrees of Libra, and the Golden Dawn gave that stretch to the Moon. The Moon has no particular standing in Libra. It isn't strong there and it isn't weakened, it's a visitor, and like most visitors it takes on the tone of the house, which in Libra belongs to Venus. So you get Libra at its freshest, cardinal air that likes to get things going and wants them fair, with the Moon's feelings running quietly under all the reasoning. The Three of Swords next along belongs to Saturn and deals in hard truths. The Four goes to Jupiter and knows how to rest. Yours is the slice that feels its way to a judgement. Justice is your Sun card, the wide view of Libra, and this is the finer grain inside it. Have a look at the woman in the picture, sitting by the water at night with both swords held across her chest.

You can tell when a room has gone off. Someone's tone shifts in a work meeting and you've registered it before they've finished the sentence, and you spend the rest of the hour adjusting what you say to bring it back level. At a family dinner you're the one who changes the subject when your dad and your sister start on politics. Picking a restaurant for a group can take you twenty minutes of texts, because you're honestly trying to find somewhere that suits everyone, the vegetarian included, and the friend who's short on money this month. When a friend asks what you think of her new boyfriend, you give her a very balanced answer and then lie awake wondering if it was the true one. Your mood follows whoever you live with more than you'd like, and a tense house tires you out faster than a long day at work does.

What people don't notice so much is your timing. The Moon gives you a feel for when someone's ready to hear a thing, and Libra gives you the words, so you tend to raise the difficult subject at the right moment, in the car on the way home or over the washing up, when nobody has to look anyone in the eye. In a fight at work about the roster, you're usually the one who sees it's really about somebody feeling overlooked, and you'll say so gently enough that they don't get defensive. People end up telling you things they haven't told their partners. I've seen this a lot with early Libra Suns. It's a skill plenty of trained counsellors spend years trying to pick up, and you mostly do it without noticing.

The one that's easy to miss is that when you don't decide, somebody else does, and it's usually whoever pushes hardest. The holiday gets booked by the friend who cared least about where you went. The job offer lapses while you're still making a list. You say 'whatever you think' to your partner and mean it, and then three weeks later you're quietly annoyed about the result and can't say so, because you did say whatever. There's a second thing too. When you're actually upset you can go very calm and very polite, arms folded, and that's hard for anyone to argue with or get through. People close to you learn that the politeness is a warning sign, but it takes them a while, and in the meantime they think everything's fine.

When something goes wrong, your first move is to go still. You're composed, you look after everyone else's feelings about it, and people tell you how well you're handling it. A week later it's showing up at three in the morning. You're going over both sides again, and you've asked four friends what they'd do, and you've half agreed with all of them. Your sleep and your appetite are usually the first things to go off with the Moon here, so watch those. The people around you can find this stage hard, because they can't tell where you stand and you keep being reasonable at them. What helps is saying how you feel out loud to one person before you've worked out whether the feeling is fair. Then eat something decent and get a proper night's sleep before deciding anything.

Libra's opposite sign is Aries, so it's common for you to be drawn to people who just say what they want, the direct type who orders for the table without a menu. That can be a relief for a while. The less obvious pattern is that early in a relationship you go along with a lot, their friends, their takeaway, their idea of a good Sunday, because it feels nice to be easy. Then about a year in, your own tastes start turning up, and your partner is a bit surprised to meet you. You also keep a quiet tally of who's giving what, which you'd never admit to. It helps to say 'let me think about it and tell you tomorrow' when you're asked something that matters. They'll get a truer answer, and you won't be holding onto a yes you didn't mean.

You're good anywhere two sides need to meet. Mediation, HR, family law, reception at a busy clinic, customer relations, design work where the client doesn't know what they want until you show them three options. Managers often use you as the person who delivers bad news, because it lands better from you, and that's worth being paid for, not just thanked. The trouble spot is any job where you have to choose between two good options on a deadline, like which supplier, which candidate, which of two proposals goes forward. You'll want more information and one more meeting. A lot of early Libras do better with a colleague who likes deciding, someone who'll say 'right, this one' after you've laid out the case. That's a real partnership, and you don't need to feel lesser for it.

At twenty this decan often takes its shape from whoever's close. You like the music your partner likes, you study what your parents think is sensible, and if someone asks what you want for dinner you honestly don't know. By the mid-thirties something has usually made the choice for you once too often, a relationship that ended on the other person's terms or a job you drifted into, and most people with the Sun here get firmer after that. They start to notice their own preferences and say them sooner. The fifties tend to bring a kind of standing in the family and at work. You become the one people bring their disputes to, and by then you're comfortable saying 'I'd rather not', which at twenty would have felt impossible.

Next time you're stuck between two options, give one heads and one tails and toss a coin. Before you look at the coin, and in the second after you do, notice what your stomach does. A little drop of disappointment or a small lift of relief is the preference you've been keeping from yourself. You don't have to do what the coin says. Try it on small things first, like which film or which café, for a couple of weeks.
